stem: A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department with 2 days of nausea, vomiting, and diffuse abdominal pain after running out of insulin. She appears lethargic with deep, rapid respirations and a fruity odor on her breath. Vitals: BP 98/62 mmHg, HR 122/min, RR 28/min, T 37.4°C. Labs: glucose 486 mg/dL, sodium 131 mEq/L, potassium 5.4 mEq/L, chloride 96 mEq/L, bicarbonate 8 mEq/L, BUN 32 mg/dL, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, arterial pH 7.12. Urinalysis shows 4+ ketones and 4+ glucose.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate initial step in management?

choices.text: Begin aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with 0.9% normal saline
choices.explanation: Patients in DKA are profoundly volume depleted (often 3-6 L deficit) from osmotic diuresis and vomiting. Isotonic saline restores intravascular volume, improves tissue perfusion, and lowers glucose by dilution and improved renal clearance. Fluids precede insulin because insulin shifts fluid and potassium intracellularly and can precipitate hypotension and hypokalemia in an under-resuscitated patient.

choices.text: Administer an IV insulin bolus immediately before any other intervention
choices.explanation: Tempting because hyperglycemia is the most visible abnormality, but starting insulin before fluid resuscitation and potassium assessment can worsen hypovolemia (as glucose and water shift intracellularly) and cause life-threatening hypokalemia, since insulin drives potassium into cells.

choices.text: Administer IV sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis
choices.explanation: Bicarbonate is generally not indicated in DKA unless pH is below approximately 6.9. The acidosis resolves as insulin halts ketogenesis and ketones are metabolized. Bicarbonate can paradoxically worsen intracellular acidosis, cause hypokalemia, and delay ketone clearance.

choices.text: Give subcutaneous long-acting insulin and admit for observation
choices.explanation: Subcutaneous absorption is unreliable in hypoperfused, volume-depleted patients, and long-acting insulin cannot be titrated to the rapidly changing glucose and electrolyte status in DKA. A continuous IV regular insulin infusion after fluids is the standard of care.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: In DKA, IV isotonic fluids come first; insulin is started only after volume resuscitation has begun and potassium status is known.

checkpoints.question: After 2 liters of normal saline, repeat potassium is 3.1 mEq/L. An insulin infusion has not yet been started. What is the most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Replete potassium IV and hold insulin until potassium is above 3.3 mEq/L
choices.explanation: Total-body potassium in DKA is severely depleted despite initially normal or high serum values, because acidosis shifts potassium extracellularly. Insulin drives potassium back into cells; starting it at a serum potassium below 3.3 mEq/L risks fatal arrhythmia from acute hypokalemia. Potassium must be repleted first.

choices.text: Start the insulin infusion now and replace potassium simultaneously
choices.explanation: Simultaneous replacement is appropriate when potassium is between 3.3 and 5.2 mEq/L. Below 3.3 mEq/L, insulin must be withheld because intracellular shift will outpace repletion and precipitate dangerous hypokalemia.

choices.text: Start insulin at double the standard rate to correct hyperglycemia faster
choices.explanation: Higher insulin rates accelerate potassium shift and glucose drop, increasing risk of hypokalemia, hypoglycemia, and rapid osmotic shifts. Glucose correction speed is not the therapeutic priority; closing the anion gap safely is.

choices.text: Give oral potassium and recheck in 6 hours
choices.explanation: This patient is vomiting and acutely ill; oral repletion is unreliable and 6 hours is far too long an interval in active DKA management, where electrolytes are typically checked every 2 hours.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Hold insulin in DKA when serum potassium is below 3.3 mEq/L; replete potassium first because insulin-driven intracellular shift can cause fatal hypokalemia.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is postoperative day 3 after right total hip arthroplasty when she develops sudden-onset dyspnea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She has no hemoptysis. Vitals: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 112/min, RR 24/min, SpO2 89% on room air, T 37.6°C. Exam shows clear lungs bilaterally, no jugular venous distention, and a tender, mildly swollen right calf. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Chest radiograph is unremarkable. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.explanation: This patient has a high pretest probability of pulmonary embolism (recent major orthopedic surgery, tachycardia, hypoxia, unilateral calf swelling). In high-probability patients, CT pulmonary angiography is the diagnostic test of choice; it directly visualizes filling defects in the pulmonary arteries and her normal renal function permits contrast.

D-dimer is useful only to rule out PE in low or intermediate pretest probability patients because of its high sensitivity but poor specificity. In a postoperative patient, D-dimer is almost universally elevated from surgery itself, and a positive result would not change the need for definitive imaging.

V/Q scanning is reserved for patients who cannot receive contrast (renal failure, contrast allergy) or when CT is unavailable. It is also less interpretable when the chest radiograph is abnormal. With normal renal function, CTPA is preferred for its speed and specificity.

Echocardiography can show right ventricular strain in massive PE and helps risk-stratify, but it is neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose PE. It is most useful in hemodynamically unstable patients too unstable to travel to CT; this patient is normotensive.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: In patients with high pretest probability of PE, proceed directly to CT pulmonary angiography; D-dimer is only useful to rule out PE when pretest probability is low.

checkpoints.question: CT pulmonary angiography confirms a segmental pulmonary embolism in the right lower lobe. The patient remains normotensive. What is the most appropriate management?

choices.text: Initiate therapeutic anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin
choices.explanation: Hemodynamically stable (submassive or low-risk) PE is treated with therapeutic anticoagulation, which prevents clot propagation while endogenous fibrinolysis resolves the embolus. LMWH or a direct oral anticoagulant is appropriate; in the early postoperative period, a parenteral agent allows tighter control if bleeding occurs.

Systemic thrombolysis is reserved for massive PE with hemodynamic instability (sustained hypotension). This patient is normotensive, and she is postoperative day 3 from major surgery, a major contraindication due to bleeding risk. Thrombolytics here would expose her to serious hemorrhage without proven mortality benefit.

choices.text: Place an inferior vena cava filter and withhold anticoagulation
choices.explanation: IVC filters are indicated when anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated or when PE recurs despite therapeutic anticoagulation. Three days after elective arthroplasty, anticoagulation is generally safe, so a filter would add procedural risk without addressing the existing clot.

Prophylactic dosing prevents new clot formation but is insufficient to treat established PE. Undertreatment risks clot propagation, recurrent embolism, and hemodynamic deterioration. Confirmed PE requires escalation to therapeutic dosing.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Hemodynamically stable PE is treated with therapeutic anticoagulation; thrombolysis is reserved for massive PE with hypotension and is contraindicated in the early postoperative period.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents with 18 hours of abdominal pain that began periumbilically and has migrated to the right lower quadrant. He reports anorexia and one episode of vomiting. Vitals: BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 96/min, T 38.1°C. Exam shows tenderness with guarding at McBurney point and pain in the right lower quadrant with palpation of the left lower quadrant. Labs: WBC 14,200/mm3 with neutrophil predominance. Urinalysis is normal.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?

choices.text: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
choices.explanation: In adult men with suspected appendicitis, contrast-enhanced CT is the confirmatory test of choice, with sensitivity and specificity above 95%. It demonstrates an enlarged appendix (>6 mm), wall enhancement, and periappendiceal fat stranding, and identifies complications such as perforation or abscess that change operative planning.

Ultrasound is the first-line imaging choice in children and pregnant women to avoid ionizing radiation, and it is highly operator dependent. In a non-pregnant adult, CT is more sensitive and less likely to be nondiagnostic, particularly with overlying bowel gas or body habitus limitations.

While classic presentations were historically taken to the operating room on clinical grounds, modern practice uses CT to reduce negative appendectomy rates and to detect complicated disease. Proceeding straight to surgery is reserved for unequivocal presentations where imaging would delay care.

choices.text: Serial abdominal exams and repeat WBC in 12 hours
choices.explanation: Observation risks progression to perforation in a patient who already has fever, focal peritoneal signs, and leukocytosis. Watchful waiting is only appropriate for equivocal presentations, not for a classic evolving appendicitis.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Contrast-enhanced CT is the confirmatory imaging of choice for suspected appendicitis in non-pregnant adults; ultrasound is preferred in children and pregnancy.

checkpoints.question: CT confirms acute uncomplicated appendicitis with a 9 mm appendix and no perforation or abscess. What is the most appropriate management?

choices.explanation: Appendectomy remains the standard of care for uncomplicated appendicitis. Laparoscopy offers faster recovery and fewer wound complications than open surgery. A preoperative dose of antibiotics covering gram-negative and anaerobic flora (e.g., cefoxitin or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole) reduces surgical site infection.

choices.text: IV antibiotics alone with planned interval reassessment
choices.explanation: Antibiotics-first strategies are a studied alternative in selected uncomplicated cases, but they carry a substantial recurrence rate (roughly one in three within a year) and higher failure rates when an appendicolith is present. On licensing exams and in standard practice, surgery remains the answer for an otherwise healthy young adult.

choices.text: Percutaneous drainage followed by interval appendectomy
choices.explanation: Percutaneous drainage applies to a contained periappendiceal abscess, typically in late presentations. This patient has no abscess to drain; the treatment for uncomplicated appendicitis is prompt appendectomy.

choices.text: Discharge with oral antibiotics and outpatient surgical follow-up
choices.explanation: Outpatient oral therapy risks progression to perforation and peritonitis. Acute appendicitis with systemic signs warrants inpatient management and definitive treatment during the same admission.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Uncomplicated acute appendicitis is treated with prompt laparoscopic appendectomy and perioperative antibiotics; drainage is reserved for contained abscesses.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with 3 days of productive cough, fever, and worsening shortness of breath. He has hypertension and drinks alcohol socially. Vitals: BP 88/58 mmHg, HR 118/min, RR 32/min, SpO2 88% on room air, T 39.2°C. He is oriented to person only. Exam reveals bronchial breath sounds and crackles over the right lower lung field. Labs: WBC 17,800/mm3, BUN 28 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL. Chest radiograph shows a dense right lower lobe consolidation.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate disposition for this patient?

choices.text: Admission to the intensive care unit
choices.explanation: He meets multiple severity criteria: confusion, BUN above 19 mg/dL, respiratory rate of 30 or more, and systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg (CURB-65 score of at least 4), plus hypoxemia. High CURB-65 scores predict substantial mortality, and hypotension with confusion signals evolving septic shock requiring ICU-level monitoring and support.

choices.text: Admission to a general medical floor
choices.explanation: A floor bed is appropriate for moderate-risk pneumonia (CURB-65 of 2), but this patient has hypotension, confusion, tachypnea, and hypoxemia. Floor-level monitoring cannot safely manage impending septic shock or respiratory failure.

choices.text: Discharge home with oral antibiotics and next-day follow-up
choices.explanation: Outpatient management applies to low-risk patients (CURB-65 of 0-1) who are hemodynamically normal and oxygenating well. Discharging a hypotensive, confused, hypoxemic patient would be a critical triage error.

choices.text: Observation in the emergency department for 6 hours before deciding
choices.explanation: This patient already meets objective ICU criteria. Delaying definitive disposition postpones aggressive resuscitation, timely antibiotics, and close monitoring, all of which are time-sensitive in severe sepsis from pneumonia.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: CURB-65 (Confusion, Urea >19 mg/dL, RR ≥30, BP <90/60, age ≥65) guides pneumonia disposition; scores of 3 or more with hemodynamic compromise warrant ICU admission.

checkpoints.question: Which empiric antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?

choices.explanation: Severe community-acquired pneumonia requires coverage of typical organisms (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae) with a beta-lactam plus atypical coverage (Legionella, Mycoplasma) with a macrolide. The combination also confers a mortality benefit in severe CAP thought to relate to macrolide immunomodulation. A respiratory fluoroquinolone with a beta-lactam is an alternative.

Macrolide monotherapy is limited to healthy outpatients in regions with low pneumococcal macrolide resistance. It is inadequate for severe CAP, where resistant pneumococcus is a real risk and mortality is high.

This regimen targets MRSA and Pseudomonas, which are concerns in hospital-acquired pneumonia or patients with specific risk factors (recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics, structural lung disease). It notably lacks atypical coverage and is unnecessarily broad for typical community-acquired disease.
Oral therapy is inappropriate in a hypotensive ICU patient with uncertain gut perfusion and absorption. Severe CAP requires IV antibiotics, and amoxicillin-clavulanate alone lacks atypical coverage.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Empiric therapy for severe CAP is an IV beta-lactam (ceftriaxone) plus a macrolide (azithromycin) or respiratory fluoroquinolone, covering both typical and atypical pathogens.

stem: A 67-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband 90 minutes after the sudden onset of right arm and face weakness with difficulty speaking. She has hypertension and takes amlodipine. She has no history of recent surgery, bleeding, or anticoagulant use. Vitals: BP 176/98 mmHg, HR 88/min irregular, glucose 108 mg/dL. Exam shows expressive aphasia, right facial droop sparing the forehead, and 3/5 strength in the right upper extremity.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate first diagnostic step?

choices.explanation: The immediate priority in acute stroke is distinguishing ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke, because thrombolysis is lifesaving in one and lethal in the other. Non-contrast CT is fast, universally available, and highly sensitive for acute hemorrhage, making it the mandatory gateway study before any reperfusion therapy.

choices.text: MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted imaging
choices.explanation: Diffusion-weighted MRI is more sensitive for early ischemia, but it is slower and less available than CT. In the thrombolysis window, every minute of delay costs neurons; MRI should not delay the decision to treat when CT can exclude hemorrhage in minutes.
Carotid imaging identifies stenosis for secondary prevention planning (e.g., endarterectomy candidacy) but plays no role in the hyperacute decision of whether to give thrombolytics.

Lumbar puncture is used when subarachnoid hemorrhage is suspected despite a negative CT. It has no role in evaluating a focal deficit consistent with ischemic stroke and would delay time-critical treatment.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Non-contrast head CT is the first test in acute stroke; its purpose is to exclude hemorrhage before considering thrombolysis, not to visualize the infarct.

checkpoints.question: Non-contrast CT shows no hemorrhage and no early infarct changes. The patient is now 2 hours from symptom onset. What is the most appropriate next step?

choices.explanation: She is within the 4.5-hour window, has a disabling deficit, no hemorrhage on CT, glucose in normal range, blood pressure below the 185/110 mmHg treatment threshold, and no contraindications such as recent surgery or anticoagulation. IV thrombolysis restores perfusion by converting plasminogen to plasmin and improves functional outcomes when given early.

choices.text: Give aspirin 325 mg and admit for observation
choices.explanation: Aspirin is standard therapy for ischemic stroke patients who are outside the window or ineligible for thrombolysis, and it is otherwise held for 24 hours after lytics. Choosing aspirin here forfeits the substantial functional benefit of reperfusion in an eligible patient.

choices.text: Lower blood pressure to below 140/90 mmHg before any treatment
choices.explanation: Blood pressure only needs to be below 185/110 mmHg for thrombolysis; hers is 176/98. Aggressive lowering in acute ischemic stroke reduces perfusion of the penumbra and can extend the infarct. Permissive hypertension is the rule unless lytics are given or pressure exceeds thresholds.

Full-dose anticoagulation has no proven benefit in acute ischemic stroke and increases hemorrhagic transformation risk. Even with her irregular pulse suggesting atrial fibrillation, anticoagulation is deferred days after the acute event.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: IV thrombolysis is indicated for disabling ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours of onset once hemorrhage is excluded and BP is below 185/110 mmHg.

checkpoints.question: The patient improves after thrombolysis. Telemetry during admission reveals paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Which long-term therapy most effectively reduces her risk of recurrent stroke?

choices.text: A direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban
choices.explanation: Atrial fibrillation causes stroke through stasis-driven thrombus formation in the left atrial appendage; these cardioembolic events are prevented by anticoagulation, not antiplatelet therapy. DOACs are first-line over warfarin in nonvalvular AF given equal or superior efficacy, lower intracranial hemorrhage rates, and no monitoring requirement.

Dual antiplatelet therapy is used short-term after minor non-cardioembolic stroke or TIA. For cardioembolic stroke from AF, antiplatelets are markedly inferior to anticoagulation and prolonged dual therapy adds bleeding risk without adequate protection.

Rate control improves symptoms and prevents tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy but does nothing to prevent thrombus formation in the atrial appendage. It is an adjunct, not a substitute for anticoagulation.
Endarterectomy benefits patients with symptomatic high-grade carotid stenosis. Her stroke mechanism is cardioembolic from AF; surgery on the carotid does not address the embolic source.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Ischemic stroke in the setting of atrial fibrillation is cardioembolic and requires long-term anticoagulation (DOAC first-line), not antiplatelet therapy.

stem: A 52-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis presents with two episodes of large-volume hematemesis over the past hour. He appears pale and anxious. Vitals: BP 92/60 mmHg, HR 124/min, RR 20/min, SpO2 96% on room air. Exam shows spider angiomata, palmar erythema, splenomegaly, and shifting dullness. Labs: hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, platelets 88,000/mm3, INR 1.7, total bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL. Two large-bore IV lines are placed and crystalloid resuscitation is begun.

checkpoints.question: In addition to volume resuscitation and preparation for endoscopy, which medications should be started now?

choices.explanation: Octreotide, a somatostatin analog, causes splanchnic vasoconstriction, lowering portal pressure and reducing variceal bleeding. Prophylactic antibiotics (ceftriaxone) are mandatory in cirrhotic patients with GI bleeding because they reduce bacterial infection, rebleeding, and mortality; bleeding disrupts the gut barrier in patients already predisposed to bacterial translocation and SBP.

Octreotide is necessary but insufficient. Omitting prophylactic antibiotics misses one of the few interventions with proven mortality benefit in variceal hemorrhage; up to 50% of cirrhotics with GI bleeding develop bacterial infection without prophylaxis.

choices.text: IV pantoprazole and observation until morning endoscopy
choices.explanation: Proton pump inhibitors are the cornerstone for peptic ulcer bleeding, but the stigmata of chronic liver disease and portal hypertension make varices the likely source. Variceal bleeding requires portal-pressure-lowering therapy, antibiotics, and urgent (not delayed) endoscopy within 12 hours.

Vasopressin lowers portal pressure but causes systemic vasoconstriction with coronary and mesenteric ischemia risk, so it has been supplanted by octreotide. Withholding antibiotics also forfeits a proven survival benefit.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Acute variceal hemorrhage is managed with octreotide plus prophylactic antibiotics (ceftriaxone) before urgent endoscopy; antibiotics independently reduce mortality.

checkpoints.question: Urgent upper endoscopy confirms actively bleeding esophageal varices. What is the most appropriate definitive intervention at this time?

choices.explanation: Band ligation mechanically strangulates the bleeding varix, achieving hemostasis in roughly 90% of cases with fewer complications than sclerotherapy (less ulceration, stricture, and perforation). It is the endoscopic treatment of choice for esophageal variceal bleeding and is repeated in sessions to obliterate remaining varices.
Sclerotherapy is effective but carries higher rates of esophageal ulceration, stricture, and perforation than banding. It is now second-line, used when banding is technically impossible.

TIPS is rescue therapy for bleeding refractory to endoscopic and medical management, or early in selected high-risk patients after initial control. Jumping to TIPS before attempting endoscopic hemostasis exposes the patient to procedural risk and worsened hepatic encephalopathy unnecessarily.

choices.text: Balloon tamponade with a Sengstaken-Blakemore tube
choices.explanation: Balloon tamponade is a temporizing bridge for massive uncontrollable hemorrhage while arranging definitive therapy. It carries high rates of esophageal necrosis and rebleeding on deflation and is never definitive treatment.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Endoscopic band ligation is the definitive first-line treatment for bleeding esophageal varices; TIPS and balloon tamponade are reserved for refractory hemorrhage.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with 3 months of unintentional 6-kg weight loss despite increased appetite, palpitations, heat intolerance, and irritability. Vitals: BP 138/72 mmHg, HR 112/min, T 37.2°C. Exam shows a fine tremor of the outstretched hands, warm moist skin, a diffusely enlarged non-tender thyroid with an audible bruit, and bilateral proptosis with lid lag. Labs: TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 3.8 ng/dL (normal 0.8-1.8).

checkpoints.question: Which finding in this patient is most specific for Graves disease as the cause of her hyperthyroidism?

choices.explanation: Ophthalmopathy is caused by TSH-receptor antibodies cross-reacting with orbital fibroblasts, stimulating glycosaminoglycan deposition and adipogenesis behind the eye. Because it reflects the autoimmune mechanism itself, proptosis occurs only in Graves disease and not in other causes of thyrotoxicosis such as toxic nodular goiter or thyroiditis.
Tremor reflects increased beta-adrenergic sensitivity from excess thyroid hormone and occurs in thyrotoxicosis of any etiology. It indicates the hyperthyroid state but not its cause.

choices.text: Suppressed TSH with elevated free T4
choices.explanation: This biochemical pattern defines primary hyperthyroidism but is common to Graves disease, toxic adenoma, toxic multinodular goiter, and the thyrotoxic phase of thyroiditis. It establishes the state, not the etiology.
Tachycardia is a nonspecific adrenergic manifestation of thyrotoxicosis from any cause and can also result from anemia, anxiety, or volume depletion.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Ophthalmopathy (and pretibial myxedema) are specific to Graves disease because they result from TSH-receptor antibody action on extrathyroidal tissues.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic management?

choices.explanation: Beta-blockade provides rapid relief of adrenergic symptoms (tremor, palpitations) and propranolol additionally inhibits peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion. Methimazole blocks thyroid peroxidase, halting new hormone synthesis, and is preferred over propylthiouracil for lower hepatotoxicity risk and once-daily dosing outside of first-trimester pregnancy and thyroid storm.

PTU is reserved for the first trimester of pregnancy (methimazole is teratogenic, causing aplasia cutis and choanal atresia) and thyroid storm (where its peripheral conversion blockade matters). Otherwise methimazole is preferred due to PTU's black-box hepatotoxicity warning.

choices.text: Immediate radioactive iodine ablation without pretreatment
choices.explanation: Radioiodine is a reasonable definitive therapy, but in this patient it is problematic upfront: it can transiently worsen thyrotoxicosis by releasing stored hormone and can exacerbate ophthalmopathy, which she has. Symptomatic control and antithyroid drugs come first, and steroid prophylaxis is considered if radioiodine is later chosen.

Levothyroxine is thyroid hormone replacement and would worsen thyrotoxicosis. This distractor tests basic recognition of the treatment direction; her TSH is suppressed by hormone excess, not deficiency.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Initial Graves therapy is a beta-blocker for symptoms plus methimazole to block hormone synthesis; PTU is reserved for first-trimester pregnancy and thyroid storm.

stem: A 28-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks gestation presents with a severe headache unrelieved by acetaminophen and new visual disturbances described as flashing lights. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated until now. Vitals: BP 168/114 mmHg confirmed on repeat measurement 15 minutes later, HR 92/min. Exam shows 2+ pitting edema of the lower extremities and brisk deep tendon reflexes. Labs: urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 0.5, platelets 142,000/mm3, AST 38 U/L, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL. Fetal heart tracing is category I.

checkpoints.question: What is the most accurate diagnosis?

choices.explanation: She has new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria, satisfying preeclampsia criteria. Severe features are defined by systolic BP of 160 or higher or diastolic 110 or higher on two occasions, or end-organ symptoms; she has both severe-range pressures and neurologic symptoms (headache, visual changes), which reflect cerebral vasospasm and edema.
Gestational hypertension is new hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria or end-organ involvement. Her proteinuria and neurologic symptoms exclude this milder diagnosis.

This is tempting because her labs (platelets, transaminases, creatinine) are near normal, but severe-range blood pressure alone (160/110 or greater) or neurologic symptoms are each sufficient to classify severe features, changing management urgency entirely.

HELLP requires hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets. Her platelets of 142,000 and AST of 38 do not meet thresholds (typically platelets below 100,000 and AST more than twice normal), though she requires monitoring for progression.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Severe-range blood pressure (≥160/110) or any end-organ symptom (headache, visual changes, RUQ pain) upgrades preeclampsia to severe features regardless of lab values.

checkpoints.question: Which combination of interventions is most appropriate now?

choices.text: IV magnesium sulfate, IV labetalol, betamethasone, and plan for delivery after stabilization
choices.explanation: Magnesium sulfate is given for eclamptic seizure prophylaxis (it raises the seizure threshold, likely via NMDA antagonism and cerebral vasodilation). Severe-range pressures require rapid-acting antihypertensives (labetalol or hydralazine) to prevent stroke. At 34 weeks with severe features, delivery is indicated after maternal stabilization, and betamethasone accelerates fetal lung maturity.

choices.text: Strict bed rest, oral nifedipine, and expectant management until 37 weeks
choices.explanation: Expectant management to term is only for preeclampsia without severe features. With severe features at 34 weeks, prolonging pregnancy risks eclampsia, placental abruption, and maternal stroke; delivery is the definitive treatment.

choices.text: IV phenytoin for seizure prophylaxis and delivery
choices.explanation: Magnesium sulfate is superior to phenytoin for preventing eclamptic seizures in randomized trials. Phenytoin is a distractor drawing on general seizure management rather than obstetric evidence.

choices.text: Emergency cesarean delivery within the next 30 minutes
choices.explanation: Preeclampsia with severe features requires delivery, but not crash cesarean when the fetal tracing is reassuring. Maternal stabilization (BP control, magnesium) comes first, and vaginal delivery via induction is often appropriate; an unstabilized operative delivery increases maternal risk.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Severe preeclampsia at ≥34 weeks is managed with magnesium sulfate, acute BP control, corticosteroids if lungs immature, and delivery after maternal stabilization.

stem: A 19-year-old college student living in a dormitory presents with 12 hours of fever, severe headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness. He vomited twice this morning. Vitals: BP 108/68 mmHg, HR 118/min, T 39.6°C. He is alert and oriented with no focal neurologic deficits and no papilledema on fundoscopy. Exam shows nuchal rigidity and scattered petechiae on the lower extremities. He has no history of immunocompromise or recent head trauma.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate immediate sequence of actions?

choices.text: Obtain blood cultures, perform lumbar puncture, then immediately start empiric antibiotics and dexamethasone
choices.explanation: He has no indications for CT before LP (no focal deficits, papilledema, seizures, immunocompromise, or altered consciousness), so LP can proceed directly. Cultures are drawn before antibiotics to preserve yield, but antibiotics must follow within minutes; every hour of delay in bacterial meningitis increases mortality. Dexamethasone given with or before the first antibiotic dose reduces neurologic sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis.

choices.text: Obtain a head CT before lumbar puncture
choices.explanation: CT before LP is indicated only with features suggesting elevated intracranial pressure or mass lesion: focal deficit, papilledema, new seizure, immunocompromise, or depressed consciousness. Routine CT in patients without these features delays diagnosis and antibiotic administration.

choices.text: Start antibiotics only after CSF Gram stain results return
choices.explanation: Waiting for CSF results before treating is a fatal error in suspected bacterial meningitis. Empiric therapy is begun immediately after cultures; the CSF profile and Gram stain then refine, not initiate, therapy.

choices.text: Perform lumbar puncture and await cell counts before deciding on antibiotics
choices.explanation: The petechial rash, fever, and meningismus in a dormitory resident make meningococcal disease a real possibility, which can progress to purpura fulminans and death within hours. Antibiotics cannot wait for laboratory confirmation.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: In suspected bacterial meningitis without red flags for elevated ICP, proceed directly to LP after blood cultures and give empiric antibiotics plus dexamethasone without delay.

checkpoints.question: CSF analysis shows WBC 2,400/mm3 with 92% neutrophils, glucose 28 mg/dL (serum 110 mg/dL), and protein 220 mg/dL. Which empiric antibiotic regimen is most appropriate for this patient?

choices.explanation: The neutrophilic pleocytosis, low CSF-to-serum glucose ratio (below 0.4), and high protein confirm bacterial meningitis. In immunocompetent patients aged 2 to 50, the dominant pathogens are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis. Ceftriaxone covers both, and vancomycin is added for possible ceftriaxone-resistant pneumococcus until sensitivities return.

Ampicillin is added to cover Listeria monocytogenes in neonates, adults over 50, pregnant patients, and the immunocompromised. A healthy 19-year-old does not need Listeria coverage; this is the classic age-based distractor.

Acyclovir treats HSV encephalitis, which typically presents with altered mental status, temporal lobe findings, and a lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis with normal glucose. The neutrophilic profile with low glucose here is bacterial, not viral.
Oral therapy is never adequate for bacterial meningitis; high-dose IV bactericidal agents are required to achieve adequate CSF concentrations across the blood-brain barrier.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Empiric therapy for bacterial meningitis in patients aged 2-50 is vancomycin plus ceftriaxone; add ampicillin for Listeria only in neonates, adults >50, pregnancy, or immunocompromise.

stem: A 19-year-old man with sickle cell disease (HbSS) is hospitalized for a vaso-occlusive pain crisis. On hospital day 2, he develops fever, pleuritic chest pain, and worsening dyspnea. Vitals: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 118/min, RR 28/min, SpO2 87% on room air, T 38.9°C. Exam reveals crackles over the left lower lung field. Chest radiograph shows a new left lower lobe infiltrate. Labs: hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL (baseline 8.5), WBC 16,400/mm3.

checkpoints.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.explanation: Acute chest syndrome is defined by a new pulmonary infiltrate plus fever or respiratory symptoms in a patient with sickle cell disease. It commonly develops 2 to 3 days into a vaso-occlusive crisis, triggered by pulmonary infarction, fat embolism from infarcted marrow, or infection, and it is the leading cause of death in adults with sickle cell disease.

Infection can trigger acute chest syndrome and the two overlap radiographically, but in a sickle cell patient mid-crisis with a falling hemoglobin, the unifying diagnosis is acute chest syndrome. Labeling it simple pneumonia understates severity and leads to undertreatment (missing transfusion therapy).

choices.text: Pulmonary embolism from deep vein thrombosis
choices.explanation: PE causes hypoxia and pleuritic pain but typically produces a clear chest radiograph, not a new lobar infiltrate with fever. In situ sickling and microvascular occlusion, not venous thromboembolism, drive this presentation.

Splenic sequestration causes rapid anemia with an enlarging spleen and hypovolemia, primarily in young children before autosplenectomy. An adult with HbSS typically has a fibrotic, nonfunctional spleen, and this presentation is pulmonary.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: New pulmonary infiltrate plus fever or respiratory symptoms in sickle cell disease defines acute chest syndrome, the leading cause of death in adult sickle cell patients.

checkpoints.question: Despite supplemental oxygen, empiric ceftriaxone and azithromycin, and analgesia, his SpO2 falls to 84% on high-flow oxygen and his respiratory rate rises. What is the most appropriate next step?

choices.explanation: Exchange transfusion rapidly lowers the HbS fraction (goal below 30%) while removing sickled cells and avoiding hyperviscosity, interrupting the cycle of sickling, vaso-occlusion, and hypoxia. It is indicated in severe or rapidly progressive acute chest syndrome with refractory hypoxemia, whereas simple transfusion suffices for milder disease.

choices.text: Simple packed red blood cell transfusion
choices.explanation: Simple transfusion is appropriate for moderate acute chest syndrome with hemoglobin well below baseline, but in severe hypoxemic disease it cannot lower the HbS percentage adequately, and raising hemoglobin much above 10 g/dL risks hyperviscosity that worsens vaso-occlusion.

choices.text: Increase IV opioids and continue current management
choices.explanation: Adequate analgesia matters because splinting from pain worsens hypoventilation, but escalating opioids in a patient with progressive hypoxemia risks respiratory depression and does not address the underlying sickling burden.
Hydroxyurea raises fetal hemoglobin over weeks to months and reduces the frequency of future crises and acute chest episodes. It has no role in the acute treatment of an evolving episode.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Severe or progressive acute chest syndrome with refractory hypoxemia is treated with exchange transfusion to rapidly reduce the HbS fraction below 30%.

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his parents for puffiness around his eyes for the past week, initially attributed to allergies, now accompanied by swelling of his legs and a tighter fit of his shoes. He had an upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago. Vitals are age-appropriate with BP 98/60 mmHg. Exam shows periorbital edema and 2+ pitting edema of the lower extremities. Urinalysis: 4+ protein, no blood. Labs: serum albumin 1.9 g/dL, cholesterol 320 mg/dL, creatinine 0.4 mg/dL, C3 and C4 normal.

checkpoints.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.explanation: This child has classic nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia. In children aged 1 to 10, minimal change disease causes roughly 90% of nephrotic syndrome. T-cell-derived cytokines injure podocyte foot processes (effaced on electron microscopy), causing selective albumin loss. Normal complement and absent hematuria support this over nephritic processes.

PSGN is a nephritic syndrome: hematuria, hypertension, and edema with low C3 about 2 to 4 weeks after streptococcal infection. This child has heavy proteinuria without blood, normal complement, and normal blood pressure, which is nephrotic, not nephritic.

FSGS causes nephrotic syndrome but predominates in adolescents and adults, particularly with obesity, HIV, or heroin use, and is more often steroid-resistant. It is the tempting alternative but is far less likely than minimal change disease at age 4.
Membranous nephropathy is the classic nephrotic lesion of adults, associated with PLA2R antibodies, hepatitis B, malignancy, and lupus. It is rare in young children.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Nephrotic syndrome in a child aged 1-10 is minimal change disease until proven otherwise; it features selective proteinuria, normal complement, and podocyte effacement.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Begin empiric oral corticosteroids without renal biopsy
choices.explanation: Because minimal change disease is overwhelmingly likely at this age and is highly steroid-responsive (over 90% remit), children aged 1 to 10 with typical nephrotic syndrome receive empiric prednisone without biopsy. Biopsy is reserved for atypical features (gross hematuria, hypertension, low complement, renal failure) or steroid resistance after 4 to 8 weeks.

choices.text: Renal biopsy before initiating any therapy
choices.explanation: Biopsy-first is the adult approach, where the differential is broad. In a typical pediatric presentation, biopsy adds procedural risk without changing initial management; steroid responsiveness itself is effectively diagnostic.
Alkylating agents are second-line for frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent disease due to gonadal toxicity, cytopenias, and malignancy risk. They are never first-line.

choices.text: Furosemide and albumin infusions alone without immunosuppression
choices.explanation: Diuretics and albumin manage symptomatic edema but do not treat the underlying podocyte injury. Without steroids, proteinuria persists, with ongoing risks of infection (urinary immunoglobulin loss) and thrombosis (antithrombin III loss).

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Typical childhood nephrotic syndrome is treated with empiric corticosteroids without biopsy; biopsy is reserved for atypical features or steroid resistance.

stem: A 66-year-old man with COPD (55 pack-year smoking history, on tiotropium and albuterol) presents with 3 days of worsening dyspnea, increased sputum volume, and a change in sputum color to green. Vitals: BP 142/86 mmHg, HR 104/min, RR 26/min, SpO2 86% on room air, T 37.8°C. He is using accessory muscles and speaking in short phrases. Exam shows diffuse expiratory wheezes and a prolonged expiratory phase. Chest radiograph shows hyperinflation without consolidation. ABG on 2 L nasal cannula: pH 7.28, PaCO2 61 mmHg, PaO2 60 mmHg.

checkpoints.question: Which initial pharmacologic regimen is most appropriate?

choices.text: Inhaled short-acting bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids, and antibiotics
choices.explanation: Moderate-to-severe COPD exacerbations are treated with short-acting beta-agonists plus ipratropium for bronchodilation, systemic corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone 40 mg for 5 days) to reduce airway inflammation and shorten recovery, and antibiotics when at least two cardinal symptoms are present including increased sputum purulence, as here. Purulence correlates with bacterial burden (H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, S. pneumoniae).

Bronchodilators are necessary but insufficient in a moderate-severe exacerbation. Omitting systemic steroids prolongs recovery and increases treatment failure, and withholding antibiotics despite purulent sputum and increased volume ignores criteria that predict benefit.

choices.text: High-dose inhaled corticosteroids in place of systemic steroids
choices.explanation: Inhaled corticosteroids are maintenance therapy for stable COPD with frequent exacerbations. In an acute exacerbation, systemic corticosteroids are required; inhaled delivery cannot achieve adequate anti-inflammatory effect in acutely narrowed airways.

Broad-spectrum coverage for MRSA and Pseudomonas is unnecessary in a typical outpatient exacerbation without risk factors (recent hospitalization, prior resistant organisms, bronchiectasis). Standard choices are amoxicillin-clavulanate, a macrolide, or doxycycline.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: COPD exacerbation treatment is short-acting bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids, and antibiotics when sputum purulence accompanies increased dyspnea or volume.

checkpoints.question: Given the ABG findings, what is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

choices.explanation: He has acute hypercapnic respiratory failure with respiratory acidosis (pH 7.28, PaCO2 61). BiPAP unloads fatigued respiratory muscles, augments alveolar ventilation to clear CO2, and reduces intubation rates and mortality in COPD exacerbations. It is the intervention with the strongest evidence base in this exact scenario, provided the patient is alert and protecting his airway.

Intubation is reserved for NIV failure, hemodynamic instability, inability to protect the airway, or depressed consciousness. This patient is awake and cooperative; jumping to invasive ventilation exposes him to ventilator-associated pneumonia and difficult weaning without first trying NIV.

choices.text: Increase oxygen to a nonrebreather targeting SpO2 of 100%
choices.explanation: Excessive oxygen in CO2-retaining COPD worsens hypercapnia through V/Q mismatch (release of hypoxic vasoconstriction), the Haldane effect, and reduced hypoxic drive. The target is SpO2 88-92%; uncontrolled high-flow oxygen can precipitate CO2 narcosis.

Methylxanthines add marginal bronchodilation at the cost of a narrow therapeutic index (arrhythmias, seizures) and are no longer recommended in routine exacerbation management. They do not address the ventilatory failure driving his acidosis.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Acute hypercapnic respiratory failure in a COPD exacerbation (pH <7.35 with elevated PaCO2) is the prime indication for BiPAP, which reduces intubation and mortality; target SpO2 is 88-92%.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with hypertension presents with 2 days of palpitations and mild exertional dyspnea. She denies chest pain, syncope, or prior similar episodes. Vitals: BP 132/84 mmHg, HR 138/min and irregularly irregular, RR 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air. Exam shows an irregularly irregular rhythm without murmurs; lungs are clear. ECG confirms atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response without ischemic changes. TSH, electrolytes, and troponin are normal. Echocardiogram shows normal ejection fraction and no valvular disease.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate initial management of her heart rate?

choices.text: IV or oral rate control with a beta-blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
choices.explanation: In a hemodynamically stable patient with AF and rapid ventricular response, first-line management is rate control with metoprolol or diltiazem, which slow AV nodal conduction. This relieves symptoms and prevents tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy while decisions about rhythm control and anticoagulation are made.

Urgent cardioversion is reserved for hemodynamic instability (hypotension, ischemia, pulmonary edema). In a stable patient with symptoms for 2 days (more than 48 hours or unknown duration), cardioversion without 3 weeks of anticoagulation or a TEE to exclude atrial thrombus risks embolic stroke.

Adenosine transiently blocks the AV node and terminates AV-node-dependent reentrant tachycardias (AVNRT, AVRT). Atrial fibrillation originates in the atria and does not depend on the AV node, so adenosine will only cause a brief pause before the rapid irregular rhythm resumes.

Digoxin slows the ventricular rate at rest but poorly during exertion, has a narrow therapeutic index, and is slower in onset than beta-blockers or diltiazem. It is an adjunct, mainly in heart failure or hypotension, not first-line in an otherwise stable patient.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Stable AF with rapid ventricular response is managed first with AV-nodal rate control (beta-blocker or diltiazem); cardioversion of AF >48 hours requires prior anticoagulation or TEE.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate long-term thromboembolism prophylaxis for this patient?

choices.text: A direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban
choices.explanation: Her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 3 (hypertension 1, age 65-74 1, female sex 1), well above the threshold of 2 at which anticoagulation is recommended for women. In nonvalvular AF, DOACs are preferred over warfarin for equivalent or better stroke prevention with roughly half the intracranial hemorrhage risk and no INR monitoring.

Aspirin provides minimal protection against the fibrin-rich, stasis-driven thrombi of AF while still carrying bleeding risk. Guidelines no longer recommend aspirin as stroke prophylaxis for AF at any risk level.

choices.text: No antithrombotic therapy given her normal echocardiogram
choices.explanation: A structurally normal heart does not eliminate embolic risk; CHA2DS2-VASc scoring is based on clinical factors, not echo findings. Her score of 3 corresponds to a meaningful annual stroke risk that anticoagulation reduces by about two-thirds.

Warfarin is reasonable when DOACs are contraindicated (mechanical valves, moderate-severe mitral stenosis, severe renal failure), but the target INR for AF is 2.0-3.0. The 2.5-3.5 range applies to mechanical mitral valves, making this doubly incorrect.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Anticoagulation in AF is guided by CHA2DS2-VASc (recommended at ≥2 in men, ≥3 in women, and considered at lower scores); DOACs are first-line in nonvalvular AF.

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with 2 days of left lower quadrant abdominal pain, low-grade fever, and constipation. She has never had similar symptoms and has never undergone colonoscopy. Vitals: BP 128/80 mmHg, HR 98/min, T 38.3°C. Exam shows focal left lower quadrant tenderness without rebound or rigidity. Labs: WBC 13,600/mm3. CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast shows sigmoid colonic wall thickening with pericolic fat stranding and no abscess, free air, or fistula.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate management?

choices.text: Bowel rest, IV antibiotics covering gram-negative rods and anaerobes, and observation
choices.explanation: CT confirms acute uncomplicated diverticulitis (wall thickening and fat stranding without abscess or perforation). Given fever, leukocytosis, and inability to tolerate intake, inpatient management with bowel rest and antibiotics covering enteric gram-negatives and anaerobes (e.g., ceftriaxone plus metronidazole) is appropriate. Selected mild cases can be managed as outpatients, some even without antibiotics.

Urgent surgery is reserved for complicated diverticulitis: perforation with generalized peritonitis, obstruction, or sepsis refractory to medical therapy. Operating on uncomplicated disease exposes the patient to major surgical risk that medical therapy avoids in the large majority of cases.

choices.text: Immediate colonoscopy to evaluate the sigmoid colon
choices.explanation: Colonoscopy during acute diverticulitis is contraindicated: insufflation and instrumentation of an inflamed, microperforated colon risks converting it to free perforation. Endoscopic evaluation is deferred until inflammation resolves.
Percutaneous drainage treats diverticular abscesses larger than about 4 cm. Her CT explicitly shows no abscess, so there is nothing to drain.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Uncomplicated diverticulitis is treated medically with bowel rest and antibiotics; surgery and drainage are reserved for complicated disease (perforation, abscess, obstruction, fistula).

checkpoints.question: She recovers fully with medical management. What follow-up is indicated?

choices.text: Colonoscopy 6 to 8 weeks after resolution of symptoms
choices.explanation: Because colon cancer can mimic diverticulitis both clinically and on CT (a perforated tumor produces similar wall thickening and stranding), guidelines recommend colonoscopy about 6 to 8 weeks after recovery in patients without a recent high-quality colonoscopy, to exclude underlying malignancy once the perforation risk of acute inflammation has passed.

choices.text: No follow-up imaging or endoscopy is needed
choices.explanation: Skipping evaluation risks missing a sigmoid cancer masquerading as diverticulitis, particularly in a 58-year-old who has never had screening colonoscopy. First episodes confirmed only by CT warrant interval endoscopic evaluation.

Repeat imaging is indicated only for clinical deterioration or failure to improve, to look for evolving abscess or perforation. In a patient who has fully recovered, it adds radiation without diagnostic value and cannot exclude mucosal malignancy.

Elective resection is no longer routinely recommended after uncomplicated episodes; it is individualized for recurrent attacks, complicated disease, or immunocompromised patients. A single uncomplicated episode does not justify colectomy.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: After a first episode of CT-diagnosed diverticulitis resolves, colonoscopy in 6-8 weeks is indicated to exclude colorectal cancer mimicking diverticulitis.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with 2 days of fever, chills, right flank pain, and burning with urination. Over the past 12 hours she has vomited four times and cannot keep down liquids. She is not pregnant (negative hCG). Vitals: BP 104/66 mmHg, HR 112/min, T 39.1°C. Exam shows right costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis: positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites, WBC too numerous to count, WBC casts present. Labs: WBC 15,800/mm3, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Urine and blood cultures are obtained.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate management?

choices.text: Hospital admission with IV ceftriaxone and IV fluids
choices.explanation: She has acute pyelonephritis (fever, flank pain, CVA tenderness, pyuria with WBC casts). While uncomplicated pyelonephritis can be treated as an outpatient, intractable vomiting makes oral therapy unreliable, mandating admission for IV antibiotics and rehydration. Ceftriaxone provides excellent empiric coverage of E. coli, the causative organism in over 80% of cases, pending culture results.

choices.text: Outpatient oral ciprofloxacin with follow-up in 48 hours
choices.explanation: Oral fluoroquinolones are appropriate for stable outpatients who can tolerate oral intake in regions with low fluoroquinolone resistance. Her repeated vomiting makes absorption unreliable, and discharging a tachycardic, febrile patient who cannot hydrate risks progression to sepsis.

Nitrofurantoin achieves therapeutic concentrations only in bladder urine, not in renal parenchyma or blood, making it strictly a cystitis drug. Using it for pyelonephritis constitutes undertreatment of a tissue-invasive infection, independent of her vomiting.

Vancomycin covers gram-positive organisms like MRSA and has no activity against E. coli and other gram-negative uropathogens that cause nearly all pyelonephritis. Empiric therapy must target gram-negative rods.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Pyelonephritis with inability to tolerate oral intake requires admission and IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone); nitrofurantoin never treats pyelonephritis because it does not achieve tissue levels.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents at his wife's urging with 6 weeks of persistently low mood, loss of interest in woodworking and coaching his son's soccer team, early-morning awakening, a 5-kg unintentional weight loss, difficulty concentrating at work, and pervasive guilt about being a burden. He admits to occasional thoughts that his family would be better off without him but denies any plan or intent to harm himself. He drinks two beers on weekends and takes no medications. Physical exam and TSH are normal.

checkpoints.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.explanation: He meets DSM-5 criteria: at least 5 symptoms for at least 2 weeks including depressed mood or anhedonia. He has both cardinal symptoms plus insomnia, weight loss, impaired concentration, guilt, and passive suicidal ideation, with functional impairment and no medical or substance cause (normal TSH, minimal alcohol).

Adjustment disorder requires an identifiable stressor with symptoms that do not meet full criteria for another disorder. He has no clear precipitant and meets full MDD criteria, which supersedes the adjustment disorder diagnosis by definition.
Dysthymia requires depressed mood for at least 2 years in adults. His symptoms span 6 weeks; the chronicity criterion is not met.
Hypothyroidism can mimic depression with fatigue, weight changes, and low mood, which is why TSH screening is standard in new depression workups. His normal TSH excludes this.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: MDD requires ≥5 symptoms for ≥2 weeks including depressed mood or anhedonia; always exclude medical mimics (hypothyroidism) and substance causes.

checkpoints.question: After assessing that he is safe for outpatient management, what is the most appropriate initial treatment?

choices.text: An SSRI plus referral for psychotherapy, with counseling that medication effect takes 4 to 6 weeks
choices.explanation: First-line treatment for moderate MDD is an SSRI (sertraline, escitalopram) combined with evidence-based psychotherapy such as CBT; the combination outperforms either alone. Patients must be counseled that antidepressant response takes 4 to 6 weeks, because early discontinuation from perceived inefficacy is the most common cause of treatment failure. Safety planning and close follow-up are essential given passive suicidal ideation.

choices.text: A benzodiazepine for symptom relief while deciding on long-term therapy
choices.explanation: Benzodiazepines do not treat depression, carry dependence and disinhibition risks, and can worsen suicidality. They have no role as monotherapy for MDD.

choices.text: A tricyclic antidepressant as first-line therapy
choices.explanation: TCAs are effective but are second-line or later because of anticholinergic burden, orthostasis, and, critically, lethality in overdose, a serious concern in any patient with suicidal ideation. SSRIs are far safer in overdose.

ECT is highly effective but reserved for treatment-refractory depression, psychotic depression, catatonia, or situations demanding rapid response (active suicidality with intent, refusal to eat). It is not initial therapy for a first moderate episode manageable as an outpatient.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Initial MDD treatment is an SSRI plus psychotherapy with explicit counseling about the 4-6 week onset of antidepressant effect; avoid TCAs in patients with suicidal ideation due to overdose lethality.

stem: A 48-year-old man is admitted for cellulitis. He reports drinking a pint of vodka daily for 15 years; his last drink was 36 hours ago. He now has tremulousness, anxiety, diaphoresis, and nausea, and states he sees insects crawling on the walls, though he knows they are not real. Vitals: BP 162/98 mmHg, HR 118/min, T 37.6°C. Exam shows a coarse tremor, diaphoresis, and mild hepatomegaly. Labs: AST 118 U/L, ALT 54 U/L, GGT elevated; glucose 88 mg/dL. He is oriented to person, place, and time.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate pharmacologic treatment for his current condition?

choices.text: Symptom-triggered benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam or chlordiazepoxide per CIWA protocol)
choices.explanation: Chronic alcohol downregulates GABA-A receptors and upregulates NMDA receptors; abrupt cessation leaves unopposed excitation. Benzodiazepines restore GABAergic tone and are the only agents proven to prevent withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens. Symptom-triggered dosing via CIWA scoring reduces total dose and duration versus fixed schedules. With his AST elevation, lorazepam (no active metabolites, non-oxidative metabolism) is a sensible agent.

choices.text: Haloperidol as primary therapy for his hallucinations
choices.explanation: His visual hallucinations with intact orientation represent alcoholic hallucinosis, part of the withdrawal spectrum. Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and do not treat the underlying GABA-NMDA imbalance; treating with haloperidol alone leaves him unprotected against seizures and DTs.

choices.text: Clonidine and propranolol to normalize vital signs
choices.explanation: Sympatholytics mask the autonomic signs used to gauge withdrawal severity while providing no protection against seizures or delirium tremens. Cosmetic vital-sign control without benzodiazepines is a classic and dangerous error.

Phenytoin is ineffective for preventing alcohol withdrawal seizures, which arise from GABA-NMDA imbalance rather than a focal epileptogenic process. Benzodiazepines are both treatment and prophylaxis.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Benzodiazepines are the only proven treatment and prophylaxis for alcohol withdrawal, its seizures, and delirium tremens; prefer lorazepam or oxazepam in liver disease.

checkpoints.question: The nurse notes he has eaten poorly for weeks and asks about starting IV dextrose fluids. What must be administered first?

choices.text: IV thiamine before or with any glucose-containing fluids
choices.explanation: Thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase; glucose loading in a thiamine-deficient patient acutely consumes remaining thiamine and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia). Chronic alcohol users are presumed deficient from poor intake and impaired absorption, so thiamine precedes dextrose.

Folate deficiency is common in alcohol use disorder and should be repleted, but it carries no acute precipitable syndrome analogous to Wernicke encephalopathy. It is routine supplementation, not the critical pre-glucose step.

choices.text: Normal saline alone is sufficient; no vitamins are needed first
choices.explanation: Saline itself is safe, but the plan is dextrose-containing fluids in a malnourished alcohol user. Omitting thiamine before glucose risks iatrogenic Wernicke encephalopathy, which is preventable and often underrecognized.

B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration over months; there is no acute interaction with glucose administration. This distractor swaps one B vitamin for the clinically urgent one.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Give thiamine before glucose in any patient with chronic alcohol use or malnutrition to prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy.

stem: A 25-year-old woman is stung by a bee at a picnic. Within 10 minutes she develops diffuse urticaria, swelling of her lips, a sensation of throat tightness, and wheezing. On EMS arrival: BP 82/50 mmHg, HR 128/min, RR 26/min, SpO2 91% on room air. She has audible wheeze and diffuse hives. She has no known allergies and takes no medications.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

choices.text: Intramuscular epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh
choices.explanation: She has anaphylaxis: acute onset with skin involvement plus respiratory compromise and hypotension after an allergen exposure. Epinephrine is the only first-line therapy; its alpha-1 effect reverses vasodilation and mucosal edema, beta-1 supports cardiac output, and beta-2 bronchodilates and stabilizes mast cells. IM injection into the vastus lateralis achieves faster, more reliable levels than subcutaneous dosing, and delay in epinephrine is the strongest modifiable predictor of fatal anaphylaxis.

Antihistamines relieve urticaria and itching but act too slowly and do nothing for airway edema, bronchospasm, or shock. Relying on antihistamines first is the most common fatal error in anaphylaxis management; they are adjuncts after epinephrine.
Corticosteroids take hours to act and their traditional rationale (preventing biphasic reactions) has weak evidence. They never substitute for epinephrine in the acute phase.

Albuterol addresses only the bronchospasm component and does nothing for hypotension or upper airway edema. It is a useful adjunct for wheezing that persists after epinephrine, not standalone treatment.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Anaphylaxis is treated immediately with IM epinephrine in the anterolateral thigh; antihistamines, steroids, and bronchodilators are adjuncts that never replace or precede epinephrine.

stem: A 15-year-old boy presents with sudden onset of severe left testicular pain that began 2 hours ago while playing basketball, accompanied by nausea and one episode of vomiting. He denies dysuria, fever, or urethral discharge. Vitals are normal except HR 104/min. Exam shows a swollen, exquisitely tender left testis lying high in the scrotum with a transverse orientation; the cremasteric reflex is absent on the left. Urinalysis is normal.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Immediate urology consultation for surgical exploration
choices.explanation: Sudden severe pain, nausea, a high-riding transversely oriented testis, and an absent cremasteric reflex make testicular torsion the working diagnosis. Torsion twists the spermatic cord, cutting off arterial inflow; testicular salvage approaches 100% within 6 hours but falls below 10% after 24 hours. With a classic presentation, surgery (detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy) should not be delayed for imaging.

choices.text: Scrotal Doppler ultrasound before any consultation
choices.explanation: Doppler ultrasound showing absent flow confirms torsion and is appropriate for equivocal presentations. When the clinical picture is classic, imaging only consumes ischemia time. This distractor tests whether the student prioritizes confirmation over salvage.

choices.text: Empiric ceftriaxone and doxycycline for epididymitis
choices.explanation: Epididymitis presents more gradually with dysuria, pyuria, and a tender epididymis, often with a preserved cremasteric reflex and pain relief on testicular elevation (Prehn sign). A normal urinalysis and abrupt onset in an adolescent argue strongly against infection; treating for epididymitis loses the testis.

choices.text: Analgesia and outpatient urology follow-up tomorrow
choices.explanation: Torsion is a surgical emergency measured in hours. Overnight delay guarantees infarction, orchiectomy, and potential impaired fertility.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Classic testicular torsion (sudden pain, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex) goes directly to surgical exploration; ultrasound is reserved for equivocal cases because salvage is time-dependent.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents with 3 days of right lower quadrant pain and light vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She has a history of chlamydia treated 3 years ago. Vitals: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 84/min. Exam shows mild right adnexal tenderness without peritoneal signs. Labs: beta-hCG 3,400 mIU/mL, hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, normal liver and renal function. Transvaginal ultrasound shows no intrauterine pregnancy, a 2.5-cm right adnexal mass without cardiac activity, and no free fluid.

checkpoints.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.explanation: A beta-hCG of 3,400 mIU/mL is above the discriminatory zone (about 1,500-2,000 for transvaginal ultrasound), at which an intrauterine pregnancy should be visible. An empty uterus at this hCG level with an adnexal mass is an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise. Her prior chlamydia is a key risk factor via tubal scarring that impairs embryo transport.

choices.text: Early viable intrauterine pregnancy not yet visible
choices.explanation: Below the discriminatory zone, an empty uterus can represent an early normal pregnancy. Above it, absence of an intrauterine sac makes a viable intrauterine pregnancy very unlikely, and the adnexal mass localizes the pregnancy to the tube.

Threatened abortion requires a confirmed intrauterine pregnancy with bleeding through a closed os. No intrauterine pregnancy is seen, so this diagnosis cannot be made and dangerously ignores the adnexal mass.

A hemorrhagic cyst can cause unilateral pain and an adnexal mass, but it does not produce a positive pregnancy test with an empty uterus above the discriminatory zone, and rupture typically shows free pelvic fluid.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: An empty uterus with beta-hCG above the discriminatory zone (~1,500-2,000 mIU/mL on TVUS) indicates ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise; PID history is a major risk factor.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate management for this patient?

choices.text: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate with serial beta-hCG monitoring
choices.explanation: She meets criteria for medical management: hemodynamically stable, unruptured ectopic, mass under 3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, beta-hCG under 5,000 mIU/mL, normal hepatic and renal function, and ability to follow up. Methotrexate, a folate antagonist, halts proliferation of trophoblastic tissue. Beta-hCG is tracked on days 4 and 7, expecting at least a 15% decline between those days.

Open emergency surgery is reserved for ruptured ectopics with hemodynamic instability. She is stable with no free fluid; subjecting her to laparotomy forfeits the fertility-sparing and morbidity advantages of medical or laparoscopic management.

choices.text: Expectant management with repeat ultrasound in 1 week
choices.explanation: Expectant management is only considered for asymptomatic patients with low and clearly falling beta-hCG (typically under 1,000-1,500). At 3,400 with an identifiable mass and symptoms, observation risks tubal rupture and hemorrhage.

D&C evacuates the uterine cavity, but the pregnancy is in the tube, not the uterus. It is occasionally used diagnostically to distinguish failed intrauterine pregnancy from ectopic when ultrasound is indeterminate, but it is never treatment for a visualized adnexal ectopic.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Stable, unruptured ectopic pregnancy with hCG <5,000, mass <3.5 cm, and no cardiac activity is treated with methotrexate and mandatory serial beta-hCG follow-up.

stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought in with 6 days of fever to 39.5°C unresponsive to antipyretics. His parents report red eyes, a rash, and irritability. Exam shows bilateral nonexudative conjunctival injection, cracked erythematous lips with a strawberry tongue, a polymorphous truncal rash, edema of the hands and feet, and a single enlarged right cervical lymph node measuring 2 cm. Labs: WBC 15,900/mm3, platelets 480,000/mm3, ESR 68 mm/h, CRP 12 mg/dL. Rapid strep and blood cultures are negative.

checkpoints.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.explanation: He meets classic criteria: fever for at least 5 days plus at least 4 of 5 features — bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes (strawberry tongue, cracked lips), polymorphous rash, extremity changes (edema), and unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy of at least 1.5 cm. Kawasaki is a medium-vessel vasculitis of young children, most common under age 5, and thrombocytosis with elevated inflammatory markers is typical.

Scarlet fever shares the strawberry tongue and rash, making it the classic mimic, but it features a sandpaper rash with pharyngitis and a positive streptococcal test, and lacks conjunctivitis and extremity edema. His negative rapid strep and conjunctival injection point away from it.

Measles causes fever, conjunctivitis, and rash, but the conjunctivitis is typically exudative or accompanied by coryza and cough, with Koplik spots and a cephalocaudal rash progression. Vaccination status and the full Kawasaki criteria constellation distinguish the two.
SJS produces mucosal involvement but with painful erosions, targetoid lesions, and epidermal sloughing, nearly always after a culprit drug. There is no drug exposure and no blistering here.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Kawasaki disease is diagnosed clinically: fever ≥5 days plus ≥4 of conjunctivitis, oral changes, rash, extremity changes, and cervical lymphadenopathy ≥1.5 cm.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate treatment, and what complication does it primarily prevent?

choices.text: IVIG plus high-dose aspirin, to prevent coronary artery aneurysms
choices.explanation: IVIG given within 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary artery aneurysm incidence from roughly 25% to under 5%, likely via broad immunomodulation of the vasculitic process. High-dose aspirin provides anti-inflammatory effect acutely, transitioned to low-dose antiplatelet therapy. Baseline and follow-up echocardiography monitors the coronary arteries. Kawasaki is a canonical exception to avoiding aspirin in febrile children.

Steroids are not first-line monotherapy; they are considered as adjuncts in high-risk patients or IVIG-refractory disease. Initial therapy in trials establishing standard of care was IVIG plus aspirin.

choices.text: Empiric ceftriaxone for presumed bacterial adenitis
choices.explanation: Anchoring on the cervical node misses the systemic criteria. Kawasaki is not infectious in a treatable bacterial sense; antibiotics do not alter its course and delay to IVIG beyond day 10 markedly increases coronary aneurysm risk.

choices.text: Supportive care only, as the illness is self-limited
choices.explanation: The fever does self-resolve, which is exactly the trap: untreated children remain at high risk of coronary aneurysms, myocardial infarction, and sudden death. Treatment exists to prevent the cardiac sequelae, not to shorten the fever.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Kawasaki disease is treated with IVIG plus high-dose aspirin within 10 days of onset to prevent coronary artery aneurysms, with echocardiographic surveillance.

stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department at night with a harsh, barking cough and noisy breathing that began after 2 days of runny nose and low-grade fever. Vitals: HR 132/min, RR 32/min, SpO2 95% on room air, T 38.2°C. Exam shows a hoarse cry, audible inspiratory stridor at rest, and mild subcostal retractions. She is alert and drooling is absent. Lungs are clear apart from transmitted upper airway sounds.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate management?

choices.text: Dexamethasone plus nebulized racemic epinephrine with observation
choices.explanation: This is croup (laryngotracheobronchitis, usually parainfluenza virus): barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor from subglottic edema. Stridor at rest with retractions defines moderate disease, warranting corticosteroids (dexamethasone reduces mucosal edema and prevents return visits) plus nebulized epinephrine, whose alpha-mediated vasoconstriction shrinks subglottic swelling within minutes. Observation for 3 to 4 hours after epinephrine watches for rebound stridor.

Steroids alone suffice for mild croup (barky cough without stridor at rest). Once stridor is present at rest, nebulized epinephrine is indicated for rapid relief, and immediate discharge skips the observation window for rebound symptoms as epinephrine wears off.

choices.text: Empiric antibiotics and lateral neck radiograph to exclude epiglottitis
choices.explanation: Epiglottitis presents with rapid-onset toxicity, drooling, dysphagia, and tripod positioning without a barking cough, and is rare in vaccinated children. She is alert without drooling after a viral prodrome; croup is viral, so antibiotics have no role, and imaging is unnecessary for a clinical diagnosis.

Intubation in croup is a last resort for impending respiratory failure (severe retractions, hypoxia, altered consciousness, fatigue). A well-appearing, alert child with moderate symptoms responds to medical therapy in the vast majority of cases.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Croup with stridor at rest is treated with dexamethasone plus nebulized racemic epinephrine, followed by 3-4 hours of observation for rebound stridor.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with 3 weeks of a new right-sided temporal headache, pain in her jaw when chewing that improves with rest, and 2 episodes of transient painless vision loss in the right eye lasting about 1 minute each. She also reports 2 months of bilateral shoulder and hip stiffness that is worst in the morning. Vitals are normal. Exam shows a tender, thickened right temporal artery with diminished pulsation. Visual acuity and fundoscopy are currently normal. Labs: ESR 96 mm/h, CRP 8.4 mg/dL, hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, platelets 510,000/mm3.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

choices.text: Start high-dose corticosteroids immediately, before biopsy
choices.explanation: She has giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms: new headache over 50, jaw claudication (the most specific symptom), amaurosis fugax, temporal artery abnormalities, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers. Transient vision loss signals ischemia of the ophthalmic artery circulation; without steroids, permanent blindness from anterior ischemic optic neuropathy can occur within days and is irreversible. With visual symptoms, IV methylprednisolone is favored; treatment must never wait for biopsy.

choices.text: Schedule temporal artery biopsy and start steroids only if it is positive
choices.explanation: Withholding treatment pending biopsy risks permanent blindness. Biopsy findings (granulomatous inflammation, giant cells) remain interpretable for at least 2 weeks after starting steroids, so therapy first, biopsy promptly after, is the rule.

choices.text: Start low-dose aspirin alone and refer to rheumatology in 2 weeks
choices.explanation: Aspirin may be an adjunct to reduce ischemic events, but it does not treat the underlying granulomatous arteritis. A 2-week delay in a patient with amaurosis fugax is an invitation to irreversible visual loss.

choices.text: Obtain MRI of the brain to evaluate the transient vision loss
choices.explanation: Amaurosis fugax here is explained by ophthalmic artery involvement of GCA, not an intracranial lesion. MRI neither confirms GCA nor changes the immediate need for steroids, and waiting for imaging wastes the treatment window.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Suspected GCA with visual symptoms requires immediate high-dose corticosteroids; never delay treatment for biopsy, which remains diagnostic for weeks after steroids begin.

checkpoints.question: Her shoulder and hip girdle stiffness is best explained by which associated condition?

choices.explanation: PMR causes symmetric aching and morning stiffness of the shoulder and pelvic girdles with elevated inflammatory markers and normal muscle enzymes. It coexists in roughly half of GCA patients, and both conditions share pathogenesis along the IL-6 axis. Recognizing the association strengthens the GCA diagnosis and informs steroid tapering.
Polymyositis causes true proximal muscle weakness with elevated creatine kinase, not stiffness with preserved strength. PMR patients hurt but are not weak, and muscle enzymes are normal.
Fibromyalgia produces widespread pain with tender points but normal inflammatory markers. Her ESR of 96 and CRP elevation are incompatible with fibromyalgia as the explanation.
RA is a small-joint symmetric synovitis of hands and feet with joint swelling. Proximal girdle stiffness without peripheral synovitis in a woman over 70 with GCA overwhelmingly favors PMR.

checkpoints.key_learning_point: Polymyalgia rheumatica accompanies about 50% of GCA cases, presenting as proximal girdle stiffness with high inflammatory markers, normal strength, and normal muscle enzymes.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency on chronic hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone presents with 2 days of vomiting and diarrhea from a gastrointestinal illness, during which she could not keep down her medications. She is now lethargic. Vitals: BP 78/46 mmHg, HR 128/min, T 38.1°C. She remains hypotensive after 2 liters of normal saline. Exam shows hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases and buccal mucosa. Labs: sodium 126 mEq/L, potassium 5.9 mEq/L, glucose 58 mg/dL, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL.

checkpoints.question: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

choices.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg plus continued isotonic saline with dextrose
